framework.name: Inversion & Pre-Mortem
framework.one_liner: Asserts that the plan has already failed completely, then works backwards to every pathway that could have produced the failure and to the safeguard that would have blocked each one.

slots.label: Goal
slots.description: The plan or outcome being protected: what a named actor has committed to do, ideally with a number and a date. This is the only slot the source reliably hands you.

slots.label: Assumed failure
slots.description: The inverted statement: it is later and the plan has failed completely and publicly. Asserted, not predicted; a fact only when the source is itself a pre-mortem.

slots.label: Failure pathway
slots.description: One concrete story of how the failure happened, told in the past tense. Not a risk category: a sequence with actors, order and a moment where the plan could no longer be saved.

slots.label: Cause
slots.description: A driver of a pathway: a condition, dependency, cost, deadline or scarce input. Often stated in the source as a constraint the speaker has already noticed and priced at zero.

slots.label: Safeguard
slots.description: The mandatory measure that blocks a pathway, written so that someone owns it and it can be checked. Never in the source, because the source has not yet imagined the failure.

relations.label: inverted to
relations.description: the goal is inverted into the assumed failure; the move that starts the exercise

relations.label: reached via
relations.description: the assumed failure is reached via this pathway

relations.label: driven by
relations.description: the pathway is driven by this cause

relations.label: guarded by
relations.description: the pathway is blocked by this safeguard

relations.label: rests on
relations.description: the source itself ties the plan, or a stated claim about it, to this stated condition, whether as a dependency the plan needs or a constraint it collides with; because the link is asserted rather than inferred, this edge can be a fact edge

examples.title: The Meridian billing go-live: a pre-mortem on an approved plan
examples.summary: The textbook use of Klein's technique. A steering meeting approves a dated go-live, records three conditions and waves off a fourth, nobody dissents, and the director closes by asserting the failure and asking for the reasons. The plan and its conditions are stated; every pathway and every safeguard is produced by working backwards from the asserted fiasco.

source.title: Final steering meeting, Meridian billing replacement
source.attribution: Written for this example around the pre-mortem procedure set out in Gary Klein, 'Performing a Project Premortem', Harvard Business Review, September 2007.
source.text: At the final steering meeting for the Meridian billing replacement, the programme director presents the plan. The new system goes live on 1 January, every customer on one platform, and the old mainframe is switched off on 31 March. The budget is 4.2 million pounds, of which 3.1 million has already been spent. The director notes three things for the record: the payments integration with the bank has never been run end to end at live volumes; two of the four engineers who wrote the old system leave in November; and the vendor's contract carries no penalty for late delivery. The finance sponsor observes that December is the busiest invoicing month of the year and asks whether January is the right date. The director answers that the date has been given to the board and to customers and will not move. Nobody in the room disagrees, and the plan is approved. Before the meeting closes the director sets one exercise: it is the following October, the programme has failed completely and publicly, and each of you has fifteen minutes to write down every reason why.

regions.label: 1 · assumed failure · it is later, the plan has failed
3 · cause · what each pathway is made of
4 · safeguard · what would have blocked it

nodes.label: Go live 1 January, all customers
nodes.text: The new billing system goes live on 1 January with every customer on one platform.
nodes.source_quote: The new system goes live on 1 January, every customer on one platform

nodes.label: Old mainframe off on 31 March
nodes.text: The old mainframe is switched off on 31 March, three months after the go-live.
nodes.source_quote: the old mainframe is switched off on 31 March

nodes.label: October: it failed completely
nodes.text: It is the following October and the programme has failed completely and publicly; the team is asked to write down every reason why.
nodes.source_quote: it is the following October, the programme has failed completely and publicly

nodes.label: What complete failure means here
nodes.text: Complete and public failure for this programme means invoices going out wrong or not at all through the winter, the mainframe kept alive past 31 March, and the 4.2 million pound budget breached with the recovery still unfunded.
nodes.rationale: The exercise asserts failure but not its content. The three stated commitments (the January cutover, the March shutdown, the budget) are the only things that can visibly break, so the concrete shape of the fiasco is read off them; the word 'publicly' points at customer-visible invoicing rather than internal slippage.

nodes.label: Payments integration never volume-tested
nodes.text: The payments integration with the bank has never been run end to end at live volumes.
nodes.source_quote: the payments integration with the bank has never been run end to end at live volumes

nodes.label: Half the old-system authors leave
nodes.text: Two of the four engineers who wrote the old system leave in November, seven weeks before the cutover.
nodes.source_quote: two of the four engineers who wrote the old system leave in November

nodes.label: Vendor has no late-delivery penalty
nodes.text: The vendor's contract carries no penalty for late delivery, so the vendor's schedule risk is entirely the buyer's.
nodes.source_quote: the vendor's contract carries no penalty for late delivery

nodes.label: December is the peak invoicing month
nodes.text: December is the busiest invoicing month of the year, immediately before the go-live date.
nodes.source_quote: December is the busiest invoicing month of the year

nodes.label: The date will not move
nodes.text: The go-live date has been given to the board and to customers and will not move.
nodes.source_quote: the date has been given to the board and to customers and will not move

nodes.label: Nobody disagreed; plan approved
nodes.text: Nobody in the room disagrees with the plan, and it is approved.
nodes.source_quote: Nobody in the room disagrees, and the plan is approved

nodes.label: Unanimity is a driver, not a signal
nodes.text: The unanimous approval is not evidence that the plan is sound: three conditions were read out and none was assigned an owner, so silence is what leaves them unmanaged.
nodes.rationale: The text records the absence of disagreement, not its reason, and gives no owner or action for any of the three conditions. Reading unanimity as a cause rather than as reassurance is the pre-mortem's characteristic move and is contestable: the room may simply have judged the risks acceptable.

nodes.label: Payments break at live volume
nodes.text: In the first week of January the payments file to the bank fails at production volume, a defect nobody could reproduce in test; direct debits are missed and the failure is visible to customers before it is understood.
nodes.rationale: Assembles the one condition the director named as untested into a sequence with a moment of no return. The source states that the integration was never run at live volumes; it does not state that it fails, when, or that customers see it first, and three unstated steps is a story, not a reading.

nodes.label: The old system's authors are gone
nodes.text: When the January reconciliation disagrees with the mainframe, the two people who could explain the old system's behaviour left in November, so every discrepancy becomes a week of archaeology and the March shutdown slips.
nodes.rationale: Joins the stated November departures to the stated March shutdown, which the source never links. The inference is that reconciliation against a system nobody understands is the long pole; plausible, but the team may have documented the old system.

nodes.label: No rehearsal window before the date
nodes.text: The only weeks in which a full dress rehearsal could have been run were December's, and December was consumed by peak invoicing on the old system, so the programme arrives at 1 January having never rehearsed the cutover.
nodes.rationale: Combines the peak-month fact with the fixed date to infer a missing rehearsal that the source never mentions. Nobody in the meeting says a rehearsal was planned or dropped; this is the pre-mortem supplying an omission rather than reading one.

nodes.label: Red status overruled by the date
nodes.text: In mid-December the programme is amber-to-red, but the date has been given to the board and to customers, the vendor bears no cost for a slip, and no one in the approving room had registered a doubt, so the go-live is ordered anyway.
nodes.rationale: Three stated conditions (the immovable date, the penalty-free vendor contract, the unanimous approval) are read together as a decision rule that no single one of them states. Contestable: a board told of a red status might well have moved the date.

nodes.label: Volume test with the bank, gated
nodes.text: Run the payments integration end to end against production-scale volumes with the bank before the code freeze, and make a passed volume test a written precondition for the go-live decision rather than a task on the plan.
nodes.rationale: Directly inverts the one condition the director named as untested. The safeguard is not in the source; the source records the gap and takes no action on it.

nodes.label: Retain two authors through March
nodes.text: Retain the two departing engineers on a paid consultancy through 31 March, and require a written reconciliation runbook from them before November, so knowledge of the old system survives the cutover.
nodes.rationale: Blocks the departure pathway at the only point where it is cheap, before the November leaving date. Nothing in the source suggests retention was considered.

nodes.label: Written abort criteria and rollback
nodes.text: Agree in writing, now, the conditions under which the January date is abandoned, name the person who may call it, and rehearse the rollback to the mainframe; a date that cannot move needs an exit that can.
nodes.rationale: Answers the pathways that all pass through the same point: a fixed date, a vendor with nothing at stake and a room that did not object. Deciding the abort rule before the pressure arrives is the standard countermeasure and is nowhere in the source.

edges.source_quote: The new system goes live on 1 January, every customer on one platform, and the old mainframe is switched off on 31 March.
The finance sponsor observes that December is the busiest invoicing month of the year and asks whether January is the right date.
The director answers that the date has been given to the board and to customers and will not move.
The director notes three things for the record: the payments integration with the bank has never been run end to end at live volumes

The director notes three things for the record: the payments integration with the bank has never been run end to end at live volumes; two of the four engineers who wrote the old system leave in November

The director notes three things for the record: the payments integration with the bank has never been run end to end at live volumes; two of the four engineers who wrote the old system leave in November; and the vendor's contract carries no penalty for late delivery
Nobody in the room disagrees, and the plan is approved.

Before the meeting closes the director sets one exercise: it is the following October, the programme has failed completely and publicly, and each of you has fifteen minutes to write down every reason why.

edges.rationale: The exercise supplies the assertion of failure; what failure looks like against these particular commitments is inferred.
The untested integration is the shortest route from the asserted fiasco back to a stated condition.
The November departures give a second, slower route to the same October verdict.
A missing rehearsal is inferred from the calendar, not stated anywhere in the meeting.
The decision-to-go-anyway pathway is the one the meeting itself sets up but never names.
A defect that only appears at production volume is exactly what an untested volume path hides.
January's first payment run carries December's peak billing, so the first live volume is also the year's largest.
The pathway is the direct consequence of losing the only people who know the system being reconciled against.
Peak invoicing consumes the same people and the same environments a dress rehearsal would need.
An immovable date removes the option of buying the rehearsal window with a short delay.
A date promised to the board and to customers is the main force behind going live on a red status.
With no penalty clause the vendor has no financial reason to warn early that the date is not achievable.
A room with no registered doubt has no record to point back to when the status turns red.
A gated volume test is the measure that would have stopped this pathway before the code freeze.
Retention plus a runbook is the only measure available before the November departures.
If the rehearsal cannot be bought, the abort rule is what limits the damage of going in unrehearsed.
Written abort criteria agreed in advance are the standard countermeasure to a date that overrules a status.

examples.title: Boom Supersonic bets the airliner on a gas turbine
examples.summary: Live from the Denver factory floor, Blake Scholl announces Superpower, a 42 MW aeroderivative gas turbine for data centres, states the ramp, the second factory, the round and the customer, and says the round is the last equity Boom will ever raise. Every number in the plan is a fact; the failure it could produce, and the safeguards that would block it, are entirely the model's work.

source.episode_title: Ellison's counter-offer, Chinese H200s, data centers in space (Aaron Ginn, Matt Kalish, Emil Michael, Blake Scholl, Naveen Rao, Ofir Ehrlich, Gorkem Yurtseven)

examples.why_this_episode: Scholl gives a factory tour that states a committed plan with numbers and dates, names the conditions it rests on, and then does the exact opposite of a pre-mortem on camera: the odds move from 'less than 50%' to 'far greater', the hardest remaining work 'feels like easy mode', and the outcome is 'basically inevitable'. That is the optimism the technique exists to invert, and the source stops precisely where the pre-mortem begins, so the assumed failure, the pathways and the safeguards are all model-supplied.

regions.label: 1 · assumed failure · it is later, the plan has failed
3 · cause · what each pathway is made of
4 · safeguard · what would have blocked it

nodes.label: Superpower: 42 MW gas turbine
nodes.text: Boom is shipping Superpower, a 42 megawatt natural-gas aeroderivative turbine for data centres, with Crusoe as the launch customer.
nodes.source_quote: a product called superpower, 42 megawatts, natural gas. It's going into data centers. Crusoe is our launch customer.

nodes.label: First 200 MW in about 18 months
nodes.text: The Denver facility they are standing in will build the first 200 megawatts of turbines over roughly the next 18 months.
nodes.source_quote: The facility we're standing in now is going to do the first 200 megawatts over the next about 18 months.

nodes.label: Second factory: 2 GW a year
nodes.text: A second factory three times the size opens early next year and is to produce two gigawatts of turbines a year.
nodes.source_quote: We're about to open early next year, another factory that is three times the size of this one. And that's what's going to be able to do two gigawatts a year.

nodes.label: Turbine cash funds Overture
nodes.text: Superpower is meant to make not just electricity but capital: the cash that finances development of the Overture supersonic airliner.
nodes.source_quote: superpower makes not just electricity, it makes capital, and it makes the capital that finances the capital-dispensive development of the overture passenger airliner.

nodes.label: 2028: both programmes stalled
nodes.text: It is 2028. Superpower shipped a fraction of the promised megawatts years late, the two-gigawatt factory stands underused, Boom is raising equity it said it would never need again, and Overture has slipped out of sight because the cash that was to fund it never arrived.
nodes.rationale: The inversion is the method's mandated first move, so the node must exist; what it says is read off the stated commitments, since the 18-month ramp, the two-gigawatt factory, the closed equity door and the airliner it funds are the only things that can visibly fail. The 2028 date and the ordering of the collapse are a judgement, and the source asserts the opposite outcome.

nodes.label: Customers will take everything made
nodes.text: Scholl says customers will take as much as Boom can possibly make, as fast as it can make it.
nodes.source_quote: We've got customers that are going to take as much as we can possibly make as fast as we can make it.

nodes.label: 300 million raised to do it
nodes.text: Boom has 300 million dollars of capital in hand to execute the ramp.
nodes.source_quote: Today we've got the capital to go do that. How much capital? 300 million.
nodes.source_ref: Blake Scholl with the hosts, L4406-L4410

nodes.label: Last equity round, ever
nodes.text: Scholl states that Boom is done fundraising and that this is the last equity round the company will ever have to do.
nodes.source_quote: So we're done fundraising. This is the last equity around we ever have to deal.

nodes.label: Reliability and scale-up named hard
nodes.text: Scholl names the remaining work: getting the turbine to work, getting it to work reliably, and getting manufacturing up to scale.
nodes.source_quote: And so there's going to be a lot of challenge and getting that to work, getting to work reliably, getting manufacturing up to scale.

nodes.label: Odds revised to 'basically inevitable'
nodes.text: Scholl says the turbine business moves Boom from less than a 50% chance of success to a far greater chance, and that supersonic flight is now basically inevitable.
nodes.source_quote: So I think this takes us from, you know, less than 50% chance of success to a far greater chance of success. I think overture supersonic flight is basically inevitable at this point.

nodes.label: Outside blades: six to nine months
nodes.text: A turbine blade sent to a traditional supplier takes six, maybe nine months to come back, from digital design to hardware.
nodes.source_quote: if we take a turbine blade and we send it to a traditional supplier to be made, it's going to take six, maybe nine months for us to get that part back, going from digital design to hardware.

nodes.label: Not enough great CNC machinists
nodes.text: Boom is hiring as fast as it can find people, and Scholl says it is hard to find enough great CNC machinists.
nodes.source_quote: It's hard to find enough great CNC machinist.

nodes.label: Permission-based approach to building
nodes.text: Scholl names a permission-based rather than freedom-to-innovate approach to building, which he says carries huge delays and huge costs, as a problem bigger than energy production.
nodes.source_quote: we have a permission-based approach to building, not a freedom to innovate approach to building.

nodes.label: The plan is priced at the good case
nodes.text: The stated confidence is itself a driver: an 18-month ramp, a second factory and a closed equity round are all sized to the case where the hard work turns out to be easy mode, so the plan carries no schedule or capital slack.
nodes.rationale: Reads the stated odds revision and the 'easy mode' framing as an input to the plan rather than as commentary on it. Scholl states the confidence and states the commitments; that the second causes the first to be under-slacked is an inference, and a founder may be publicly confident while planning privately for the bad case.

nodes.label: The 200 MW ramp slips a year
nodes.text: The first units take longer than planned: hot-section parts that turn in a day in Denver still queue behind machines and machinists that cannot be hired fast enough, permits for the second building slip, and 18 months becomes 30, so the ramp arrives after the customers have signed elsewhere.
nodes.rationale: Assembles four separately stated constraints (part turnaround, scarce machinists, permission-based building, manufacturing scale-up) into one schedule failure. Each ingredient is quoted; the assembly and the doubling of the timeline are not in the source, and Scholl argues the opposite.

nodes.label: Launch customer's own build slips
nodes.text: Crusoe is the only customer named, and its demand comes from the same AI capex cycle that funds Boom; when that cycle pauses, or Crusoe dual-sources to an incumbent for financing reasons, the two-gigawatt factory's fixed cost lands years before its revenue does.
nodes.rationale: Nobody in the source hints at demand risk; Scholl says the opposite, that customers will take everything Boom can make. Concentration on a single named counterparty exposed to the same cycle is the model's own reading of the announcement and is entirely contestable.

nodes.label: A field failure freezes the order book
nodes.text: A turbine fails in service at a live data centre in year two. The engine is new, the operator's uptime commitments are not, and while the root cause is chased every prospect waits for someone else to go first, so orders stop at exactly the moment the second factory comes online.
nodes.rationale: Scholl names reliability as one of the two biggest challenges, so the ingredient is stated; the failure in service, its timing against the factory opening and the freeze in the order book are the model's construction.

nodes.label: Turbine slip stops the airliner too
nodes.text: Because the airliner is funded out of turbine cash and the equity door was publicly closed, any turbine delay converts one to one into an Overture delay; the company must either reopen a round it said it would never need or slow the programme the turbine was built to accelerate.
nodes.rationale: The coupling is stated outright, and so is the decision to stop raising equity; that the coupling propagates failure in both directions, rather than only cash in one, is the inference. Pre-mortems on each programme separately would miss it.

nodes.label: Guarantee the 24-hour part turn
nodes.text: Make the in-house 24-hour turn on hot-section parts a contractual capacity commitment rather than a happy property of one building: a second machining cell on a separate site and one qualified external supplier held on retainer, so a single machine, fire or permit cannot stop the ramp.
nodes.rationale: Attacks the schedule pathway at the input Scholl himself identifies as the industry's binding constraint. Redundancy for an advantage that currently exists in exactly one building is nowhere in the source.
nodes.idea: The six-to-nine-month industry lead time for hot-section parts is a market: a rapid-turn superalloy parts service, printing, heat-treating and machining turbine blades in 24 hours, sold to every turbine and engine builder that sold off its own supply chain.

nodes.label: Bond delivery and uptime to customers
nodes.text: Sell the turbine with a delivery-and-uptime bond: a third party underwrites the schedule and the availability so a data-centre developer can buy from an unproven vendor without carrying the whole risk, which also removes the reason a launch customer would quietly dual-source.
nodes.rationale: Addresses the customer-concentration and field-failure pathways at the same point, the buyer's inability to price a new vendor's risk. Contestable as a safeguard because the bond costs money the plan has not budgeted, and nothing in the source suggests customers asked for one.
nodes.idea: Behind-the-meter power is bottlenecked on trust, not turbines: an underwriting product that bonds delivery dates and uptime for new energy-hardware vendors would let data-centre developers buy from anyone but GE and Rolls-Royce.

nodes.label: Ring-fence airliner from turbine cash
nodes.text: Separate the two programmes financially before the coupling is tested: fund Overture to a named milestone from the round already raised, and write down in advance the trigger, the size and the terms of the equity raise that the public 'never again' commitment would otherwise delay past the point of usefulness.
nodes.rationale: The coupling and the closed equity door are both stated; the safeguard is to decide the exception now rather than under distress. Standard practice for a programme funded by another programme's cash flow, and absent from the source.

nodes.label: Pre-permitted sites off the shelf
nodes.text: Take the permission-based approach Scholl names as a constraint off the critical path by pre-clearing air and interconnect permits for the first deployment sites and for the second factory before the machines are ordered, so the schedule is set by manufacturing rather than by a queue.
nodes.rationale: Turns a general complaint about American permitting into a specific measure on this plan's critical path. Speculative in that the source never says permits are on Boom's critical path, only that they slow anyone building physical things.
nodes.idea: Pre-permitted, grid-adjacent turbine pads sold as a shelf product, with air and interconnect approvals already granted, would let a data-centre developer buy months rather than wait in a permitting queue.

edges.rationale: Scholl asserts the demand and, separately and hundreds of lines earlier, the 200 megawatt ramp; he never says the ramp depends on the demand holding. Reading the two as a dependency is the model joining adjacent claims in one turn, which SPEC 3 classes as derived.

edges.source_quote: We've got customers that are going to take as much as we can possibly make as fast as we can make it. Today we've got the capital to go do that.
we can now take that same engine core, put a power turbine on it, and get to profitability years faster
to have raised the round that lets us ship the revenue, new product that then produces the cash to fund the rest of the stuff. So we're done fundraising.
So this is basically the first unit of what we will copy paste into the facility that will do 2 gigawatts per year.

the single biggest challenges we had were how do we prove that we have a reliable engine, and where do we get all the money to do it? And running the sting on the ground proves the engine is reliable, and it literally prints the cash that we need to go develop the airplane.

edges.rationale: The nearest dated commitment is the one the assumed failure negates first.
Inverting the stated purpose, not only the milestone, is what makes the failure complete rather than a slip.
Schedule is the route with the most stated ingredients and the fewest new assumptions.
Demand risk is the route the source explicitly denies, which is why the pre-mortem has to supply it.
Reliability is named by the speaker as a live challenge, so this route starts from a stated condition.
The coupling between the two programmes turns any single-programme failure into the complete one.
Part turnaround is the constraint Scholl himself identifies as what sets iteration speed in this industry.
A factory that runs 24-7 on CNC work is rate-limited by the machinists it cannot find.

Scholl names permitting as the biggest problem with building physical things, but never says it sits on Boom's own critical path; treating it as a driver here is the model's extension of a general complaint to this plan.
Getting manufacturing up to scale is stated as remaining work, and unfinished scale-up is what a ramp slip is made of.
A schedule with no slack turns each of the other drivers into a delay rather than an absorbed variance.
Unlimited demand asserted from one named customer is the assumption this pathway breaks.
Sizing a two-gigawatt factory to the good case is what makes a demand pause fatal rather than inconvenient.
The speaker names reliability as one of the two biggest challenges; this pathway is that challenge losing.
An 'easy mode' framing of the remaining engineering is what would license shipping before the duty-cycle evidence is in.
A publicly closed equity door is what removes the obvious remedy for a turbine delay.
300 million funds a ramp on plan; it is the size of the buffer that decides whether a slip is survivable.
Calling the airliner basically inevitable is what makes a coupled dependency feel like an accelerator rather than a risk.
Redundant fast part turnaround is the measure that keeps a single-site advantage from becoming a single point of failure.
Pre-clearing approvals is the only way to take a permitting queue off a manufacturing schedule.
A bonded delivery commitment is what lets a second and third customer sign before the track record exists.
An underwritten uptime commitment converts a field failure from a market freeze into a claim.
Deciding the funding exception in advance is what stops a public commitment from becoming a delay.
